analysis.one_liner: Toughens environmental and product-safety standards to protect children from toxic pollutants and chemicals.
analysis.headline: Introduced in the Senate in September 2006 with no cosponsors, the bill was sent to the Environment and Public Works Committee and never received a hearing, a vote, or any further action before that Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required the EPA and other agencies to set pollution and chemical-safety standards that explicitly protect children, adding an extra 10-fold safety margin whenever data on a chemical's effects on children are missing. It would have created public lists of substances dangerous to children, forced manufacturers of toys and other products to report toxic chemicals in them, lowered reporting thresholds for releases of chemicals like lead, mercury, dioxin, cadmium, and chromium, let citizens sue violators, and paid states to test schools and day care centers for pollutants and remove them. It never left committee.
analysis.who_benefits: Children, pregnant women, the elderly, and people with serious illnesses, who would gain stronger health standards with an added margin of safety for pollutants [S3]. Parents and communities near Superfund sites would get exposure registries and right-to-know information [S3]. Families would learn which products contain chemicals toxic to children through public reporting [S3]. States and local schools would get federal grants to test for and remove pollutants from schools and day care centers [S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Children, families, and communities near toxic sites

how_it_helps.text: Requires every environmental and public health standard set by the EPA to protect children and other vulnerable groups with an adequate margin of safety, and adds an extra 10-fold safety factor whenever data on a chemical's toxicity to children is lacking [S3].

Directs the EPA to publish peer-reviewed lists of pollutants and substances with known or suspected risks to children, along with lists of safer-for-children alternatives, updated annually and made available to the public online [S3].

Requires manufacturers and importers of children's products to report to the Consumer Product Safety Commission any listed toxic chemicals in their products, with the information published annually in the Federal Register and made available electronically to the public [S3].

Requires the EPA to set reporting thresholds for toxic releases of lead, mercury, dioxin, cadmium, chromium, and other persistent chemicals so that at least 80 percent of releases are publicly reported [S3].
Authorizes private citizens to sue companies that violate the product-reporting rules and the agency when it fails to act, with penalties going into a fund for enforcement [S3].

Establishes a block grant program for states that pass laws requiring testing of school and day care sites for environmental pollutants, funding testing and removal of pollutants found on those properties [S3].

Creates a national registry of children exposed to significant levels of hazardous substances released at Superfund-listed facilities, and funds children's environmental health education and training programs [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Chemical manufacturers and pesticide makers, who would face new testing requirements, research costs, stricter safety margins, and broader public disclosure of toxic releases [S3]. Toy makers and importers of children's products, who would have to test for and publicly report toxic chemicals in their goods and face citizen lawsuits and penalties for failures [S3]. Federal taxpayers, since the bill authorizes 'such sums as are necessary' for the research and grant programs without setting a budget [S3].

drawbacks.text: The mandatory 10-fold safety margin whenever child-specific data are missing could effectively exclude many substances from use even where they are safe at normal exposure levels, since the burden of generating the data falls on manufacturers [S3].
The bill authorizes unlimited appropriations for research, toxicological profiles, registries, and state block grants, with no cost estimate attached [S3].
Expanded citizen lawsuits with attorney-fee awards and shifted burdens of proof would increase litigation exposure for product makers, costs that could be passed on in prices [S3].
Duplicating safety review across four separate environmental statutes could create overlapping agency mandates and slow standard-setting [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's core idea — that children are more vulnerable to pollutants than adults and that uncertainty should err on the side of protection — is well supported by the bill's own findings on differing child metabolism and exposure [S3]. Its disclosure, testing, and grant provisions would have given parents real information and cleaner schools. The costs are real but ordinary for environmental regulation: more industry testing and reporting, open-ended federal spending, and a possible overreach from the automatic 10-fold margin. The bill was ambitious and duplicative in places, but the burden it would have imposed fell mainly on manufacturers whose products reach children.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in the final weeks of the 109th Congress, referred to the Environment and Public Works Committee, and sat there with no hearing or vote until that Congress ended on January 3, 2007 [S1][S5].

narrative.text: Senator Robert Menendez introduced the bill on September 29, 2006, in the closing weeks of the two-year Congress [S1][S5].
No senator signed on as a cosponsor [S4].
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Environment and Public Works on the day of introduction [S5].
The committee took no further action on the bill — no hearing, no markup, no report — and it never reached the Senate floor for a vote [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Chemical, pesticide, and toy manufacturers came out ahead, since the testing, disclosure, and reporting requirements that would have applied to them never took effect. Families gained nothing, because the bill never advanced past referral.

for.name: Sen. Robert Menendez
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to the Environment and Public Works Committee; it was his bill alone, with no cosponsors

against.name: Senate Environment and Public Works Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and took no further action — no hearing, no markup, no vote — before the Congress ended

against.name: James Inhofe
against.role: Chair, Senate Environment and Public Works Committee (109th Congress)
against.what_they_did: As chairman, never scheduled the bill for committee consideration during the three months it sat in the panel

sides.party_line_note: With one sponsor and zero cosponsors, no bloc ever lined up for or against the bill; it died in committee without any recorded vote.

industries.note: The bill would force new child-focused testing strategies, broader public reporting of toxic releases (including lead, mercury, dioxin, cadmium, and chromium at lower thresholds), and stricter 10-fold safety margins in standards [S3]. Because the bill died, these requirements never took effect.

industries.industry: Toy and children's product makers and importers
industries.note: Manufacturers would have to test for and publicly report carcinogenic, neurotoxic, or reproductive-toxic chemicals in products intended for children, and would face citizen lawsuits and penalties for noncompliance [S3]. The bill's death left the pre-existing rules in place.

The bill states a policy of eliminating dangerous pesticide use in schools and day care centers and directs federal research into pesticide toxicity and exposure in children, with the cost of research borne by manufacturers and processors [S3].

industries.industry: Toxicology testing and environmental consulting firms
industries.note: Mandated chemical testing, site testing at schools and day care centers, and state grant programs would have created paid testing and remediation work [S3].
